## The Human Mortality Database release

All analyses use the period life tables of the
[Human Mortality Database](https://www.mortality.org) (HMD).  The HMD is
revised continually — new years are added and past estimates are sometimes
corrected — so "the HMD" is not a fixed data set.  To make the analysis
reproducible we therefore pin one specific **release**: the bulk download
("all statistics" zip archive) dated **29 October 2026**.

The HMD licenses its estimates (life tables, death rates, exposures) under
CC BY 4.0, but asks users to obtain the data from its website rather than
from third parties.  This repository therefore does **not** contain the data.
You download the zip yourself (a free registration is required) and save it,
unopened and unrenamed apart from the name below, as

```
raw/hmd/hmd_statistics_20261029.zip
```

The file `raw/MANIFEST.json` — which *is* part of the repository — records
the release, where it came from, and SHA-256 checksums of the zip and of the
four files inside it that the analysis reads.  A checksum is a 64-character
fingerprint of a file's exact bytes: if a single byte differs, the
fingerprint differs.  Verifying it proves that you are running the analysis
on exactly the data the paper used.

```{python}
#| label: d1-setup
#| code-summary: "Chapter setup: imports and provenance tracking"

# Every chapter starts the same way: import the project package, declare
# which chapter is running (so every artefact, figure, table and number it
# produces is attributed to it), and load the analysis parameters.
import json

import pandas as pd

from mdmx import artifacts, data, latex, paths, provenance
from mdmx.config import params

provenance.start_chapter("d1-acquire")
P = params()
print(f"Project root : {paths.root().name}/")          # the folder's name: the full path is the reader's own
print(f"HMD release  : {P.data.hmd_release}")
```

## The manifest

```{python}
#| label: d1-manifest
#| code-summary: "Show what the manifest says about the release"

manifest = json.loads((paths.raw() / "MANIFEST.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
release = manifest["hmd"][P.data.hmd_release]
released = pd.Timestamp(P.data.hmd_release)
latex.report("dataReleaseDate", f"{released.day} {released:%B %Y}", desc="Date of the HMD release used")
latex.report("dataReleaseDoi", release["doi"], desc="Version DOI of the HMD release used")
for key in ("title", "source_url", "file", "zip_sha256", "zip_bytes",
            "last_modified_stamp", "downloaded", "license"):
    print(f"{key:>20s} : {release[key]}")
print("\nFiles read from inside the zip, with their SHA-256 checksums:")
for member, digest in release["members"].items():
    print(f"  {member:<45s} {digest}")
```

Only four of the 176 files in the archive are used: the female and male
1×1 period life tables (single years of age by single calendar years), and
the 1×1 death counts and exposures to risk, which the adaptive pooling step
needs (chapter d5).

## Verifying the release

`mdmx.data.verify_release()` locates the release and recomputes every
checksum.  It accepts either the zip exactly as downloaded or — for
convenience — a folder `raw/hmd/20261029/` holding just the four files with
their paths as inside the zip.  In both cases each of the four files must
match the manifest, and if the zip is present its own checksum must match
too.  Any mismatch stops the pipeline with an error.

```{python}
#| label: d1-verify
#| code-summary: "Verify the checksums and register the release as the root artefact"

report = data.verify_release(P.data.hmd_release)
print(f"Release found at: {report['source']}")
if report["zip_sha256"]:
    print(f"Zip checksum     : OK ({report['zip_sha256'][:16]}…)")
for member, res in report["members"].items():
    print(f"  {member:<45s} {'OK' if res['ok'] else 'MISMATCH'}")

# Record the verified release as the root of the provenance graph.  Its
# content is the release label and the checksums of the four member files —
# deliberately NOT the file location or the zip's own checksum, so that the
# cache is identical whether the data were read from the zip or from an
# extracted folder, on any computer.  Every downstream artefact is thereby
# tied to exactly these bytes.
artifacts.save(
    "hmd_release",
    {"release": P.data.hmd_release,
     "members": {m: r["sha256"] for m, r in report["members"].items()}},
    params={"release": P.data.hmd_release},
    desc="Verified HMD bulk release: checksums of the four files used",
)
```

## The populations

The HMD covers 50 populations in this release.  Several are not
independent: the United Kingdom total (GBR_NP) contains England & Wales,
Scotland and Northern Ireland; Germany (DEUTNP) contains East and West
Germany for the years they overlap; and New Zealand (NZL_NP) contains its
Māori and non-Māori populations.  The HMD also publishes *civilian-only*
series for France and England & Wales, which omit military deaths in war
years.  The register below records these relationships; it lives in
`config/populations.csv`, so it can be read and edited without touching code.

```{python}
#| label: d1-populations
#| code-summary: "The population register"

pops = data.load_populations()
artifacts.save("populations", pops, inputs=["hmd_release"],
               desc="Population register: HMD codes, names, aggregates, inclusion")
pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 60)
used = pops[pops["included"] == "yes"]
latex.report("dataNCountries", int((used["aggregate_of"] == "").sum()),
             desc="Countries and territories: the populations used that are not part of another")
pops
```

The two civilian series are excluded (`included = no`), leaving
`{python} len(used)` populations.  The overlapping aggregates are *kept*, as in the paper: each is
a population in its own right.  The consequences — some populations count
twice in the decomposition, and their forecast errors are not independent —
are discussed in the paper (§2.1, and §11.5, "Limitations").

```{python}
#| label: d1-end
#| code-summary: "Close the chapter"
latex.write_numbers()
provenance.end_chapter();
```
